The proof combines a conditional exponential-moment bound with deterministic propagation through the corrected observable moment region.  If \(B\in\{0,1\}\) has mean \(q\), put \(\psi(\lambda)=\log E\exp\{\lambda(B-q)\}\).  Exponential tilting preserves a Bernoulli law, so \(\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0\) and
\[
\psi''(\lambda)=q_\lambda(1-q_\lambda)\leq\frac14.
\]
Taylor's formula with integral remainder therefore gives
\[
E\exp\{\lambda(B-q)\}\leq\exp(\lambda^2/8).
\]
For \(N>0\) independent copies, Markov's inequality applied separately to the two tails and optimized at \(|\lambda|=4r\) yields
\[
\Pr(|\bar B_N-q|>r)\leq2e^{-2Nr^2}.                                  \tag{31}
\]

Conditional on \(N_{zx}=N>0\), the observations selected into cell \((z,x)\) are independent draws from the conditional law given \((Z=z,X=x)\).  Hence, with
\[
r_{zx}=\sqrt{\frac{\log(2J/\alpha)}{2N_{zx}}},
\]
equation (31) bounds the unconditional failure probability of each cellwise primitive interval by \(\alpha/J\), after averaging over \(N_{zx}>0\).  If \(N_{zx}=0\), the interval is \([0,1]\) and cannot fail.  Applying (31) with \(N=n\) gives the same bound for each interval covering \(p_x\) around \(\widehat p_x\).  Since \(J\) counts all cellwise primitive intervals and all covariate-mass intervals, the unconditional union bound gives, uniformly over the maintained laws,
\[
\inf_P\Pr_P(\mathscr E_n)\geq1-\alpha.                               \tag{32}
\]
The positive-cell support and treatment-overlap premises used by the established IPCW-recovery lemma imply \(\Pr(Z=z,X=x)>0\), so every population conditional moment is defined.  No positive lower bound on a realized \(N_{zx}\) is used.

Fix \((z,x)\).  The corrected finite cells
\[
I_i=[a_i,a_{i+1})\quad(0\leq i<m-1),
\qquad I_{m-1}=[a_{m-1},\tau],
\]
together with \(D(z)>\tau\), are disjoint and exhaustive for the death coordinate.  Thus the true nonnegative table satisfies
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_j\pi^{zx}_{ij}+\sum_j\pi^{zx}_{\infty j}=1,       \tag{33}
\]
including every allowed atom at \(D(z)=\tau\).  By arm-specific independent censoring,
\[
A^{zx}_{ij}=\int_{I_i\times B_j}G_{zx}(d)\,\mu_{zx}(d d,d r).
\]
For \(i<m-1\), \(a_i\leq d<a_{i+1}\) on \(I_i\); for \(i=m-1\), \(a_{m-1}\leq d\leq a_m=\tau\).  Since \(G_{zx}\) is nonincreasing, in both cases
\[
g^{zx}_{i+1}\pi^{zx}_{ij}
\leq A^{zx}_{ij}
\leq g^{zx}_i\pi^{zx}_{ij}.                                         \tag{34}
\]
In particular, the contribution of \(D(z)=\tau\) in the last bin is multiplied by \(G_{zx}(\tau)=g^{zx}_m\); it is neither discarded nor assigned the left-endpoint censoring probability.  No exact-bin equality is used.

At deterministic \(a_i\), for \(0\leq i<m\), conditional censoring independence and the left-closed bin convention give
\[
Y^{zx}_i=g^{zx}_i\left\{\sum_{h\geq i,j}\pi^{zx}_{hj}
 +\sum_j\pi^{zx}_{\infty j}\right\}.
\]
Likewise, horizon completion requires \(D(z)>\tau\), and hence
\[
V^{zx}_j=g^{zx}_m\pi^{zx}_{\infty j}.                               \tag{35}
\]
By the survival-function definition and full-horizon censoring support,
\[
1\geq g^{zx}_0\geq\cdots\geq g^{zx}_m\geq\gamma>0.                  \tag{36}
\]
The semicompeting order inherited from \(\mu_{zx}\) supplies the table's event-order restrictions.  On \(\mathscr E_n\), every true observable moment and every \(p_x\) lies in its stipulated interval.  Equations (33)--(36) therefore put the true coarsened primitive and censoring vectors in \(\mathcal B_n\).

Now take a surface in \(\Theta_I(P)\), represented by \((\nu_x:x\in\mathcal X)\), and coarsen \(D(0)\), \(D(1)\), and the readmission mark with the same ordered cells.  Write \(c_m(d)\) for the resulting ordered death category, including the residual category \(D>\tau\).  Its projected table has the true coarsened margins.  Terminal monotonicity implies
\[
\{c_m(D(0))>k,R(1)\in B_j\}
\subseteq
\{c_m(D(1))>k,R(1)\in B_j\},
\]
because the corrected cells are ordered and \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  Consequently, for every chain cut \(k\) and mark bin \(j\),
\[
\sum_{i>k}f^x_{ij}
=\Pr\{c_m(D(0))>k,R(1)\in B_j\mid X=x\}
\leq\Pr\{c_m(D(1))>k,R(1)\in B_j\mid X=x\}
=\kappa^x_{kj}.                                                       \tag{37}
\]
The quadratic chain-flow theorem makes these inequalities and the two margins an exact feasible grid image.  Because the true primitive vector is in \(\mathcal B_n\) on \(\mathscr E_n\), the union defining \(\mathcal C_n\) yields
\[
\Theta_I(P)|_{\mathcal G_m}\subseteq\mathcal C_n
\qquad\text{on }\mathscr E_n.                                      \tag{38}
\]
Combining (32) and (38) proves
\[
\inf_P\Pr_P\{\Theta_I(P)|_{\mathcal G_m}\subseteq\mathcal C_n\}
\geq1-\alpha.
\]
The argument propagates one simultaneous primitive event and does not differentiate the optimized flow value.  It therefore remains valid when several cuts tie or the active flow face changes.

The proof uses nested-deadline matching, suffix cuts, and compact limiting.  Fix \(x\) and \(t\in[0,\tau]\), write \(s=s_x(t)\), and use the boundary convention \(K_x(\infty,B)=s_x(\infty)=0\).  If \(s=0\), monotonicity of \(s_x\) gives \(s_x(u)=0\) for every \(u\geq t\); the cut at \(u=\infty\), together with nonnegativity, makes both deadline ranks zero.  Hence the unstandardized claim is immediate.  Assume below that \(s>0\).

For any compatible full law, let \(w\) be the treated-record submeasure selected by \(D(0)>t\):
\[
w(H)=\Pr\{(D(1),R(1))\in H,D(0)>t\mid X=x\}.
\]
It has mass \(s\), is dominated by \(\mu_{1x}\), and is supported on \(D(1)>t\).  For every \(u\geq t\), terminal monotonicity gives
\[
w(D(1)>u)\geq\Pr(D(0)>u\mid X=x)=s_x(u).                             \tag{12}
\]
For a Borel mark set \(B\), split the selected records at deadline \(u\).  Equation (12) permits at most \(s-s_x(u)\) selected records at or before \(u\), while domination by \(\mu_{1x}\) permits at most \(K_x(u,B)\) available \(B\)-marked records after \(u\).  Therefore
\[
w(R(1)\in B)\leq s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,B).
\]
This also holds at \(u=\infty\) by the declared boundary convention.  Taking the infimum gives the upper deadline bound.

We next prove sharpness on a finite rational grid.  Multiply every mass by a common denominator.  Make one demand copy for each unit of control mass with \(D(0)>t\) and one resource copy for each unit of treated mass with \(D(1)>t\).  Join a demand at death level \(i\) to a resource at death level \(h\) precisely when \(i\leq h\).  Taking the full mark set in the survivor-capacity inequalities gives every suffix condition
\[
\#\{\text{resources later than }u\}
\geq\#\{\text{demands later than }u\}.                              \tag{13}
\]
Sorting demands from latest to earliest and assigning an unused admissible resource at each step proves by induction from (13) that all demands can be matched.

Fix a mark set \(B\).  Starting from a full matching, use alternating-path augmentation to maximize the number of selected \(B\)-resources.  Because demand neighborhoods are nested suffixes, if no augmentation is possible, the demands reached by alternating paths may be enlarged to the suffix beginning at their earliest death level without enlarging their resource neighborhood.  At the stopping suffix \(u\), every selected \(B\)-resource is either used by a demand at or before \(u\), of which there are \(s-s_x(u)\) after rescaling, or is an available \(B\)-resource after \(u\), of which there are \(K_x(u,B)\).  Thus equality is attained in the smallest of the valid cut bounds
\[
\#\{\text{selected \(B\)-resources}\}
\leq\#\{\text{demands at or before }u\}
 +\#\{\text{available \(B\)-resources after }u\}.                 \tag{14}
\]
Hence the maximum selected \(B\)-mass is \(\min_u\{s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,B)\}\).  Superposing the maximizing partial matching with a full matching and augmenting on alternating paths and cycles extends it to a full survivor-demand matching without deleting a selected \(B\)-resource.

The family of matchable resource subsets has the augmentation property.  Indeed, superpose matchings of two matchable sets of different sizes.  A component starting from a resource used only by the larger matching must be an alternating path with an unmatched endpoint, and switching that path augments the smaller set.  Order resources by increasing readmission category and greedily retain a resource exactly when the retained set remains matchable.  The augmentation property implies after each prefix that the retained set has maximum cardinality among resources in that prefix.  Extending the final retained set to a matching of all survivor demands therefore produces one coupling attaining the upper cut formula simultaneously for every readmission prefix.  Reversing the mark order maximizes every complementary suffix and hence produces one coupling minimizing every prefix simultaneously.

The unselected treated records can be paired with control deaths at or before \(t\).  Put \(T_x(u)=\Pr(D(1)>u\mid X=x)\).  For \(u\leq t\), every selected resource has \(D(1)>t\), so its tail mass at \(u\) is \(s\).  The residual treated and control tails are respectively \(T_x(u)-s\) and \(s_x(u)-s\).  Taking the full mark set in the survivor-capacity inequality gives \(T_x(u)\geq s_x(u)\), and hence
\[
T_x(u)-s\geq s_x(u)-s.                                               \tag{15}
\]
For \(u>t\), the residual control tail is zero.  The same latest-to-earliest suffix induction therefore completes the terminal-monotone matching without changing the selected cohort.

For arbitrary real masses on a finite grid, approximate the table within its finite system of margin and capacity constraints by rational feasible tables.  Their extremizers lie in a fixed finite simplex.  A convergent subsequence preserves nonnegativity, both margins, the closed terminal order, every finite cut, and the objective.  This proves the deadline formula and the simultaneous-prefix assertion for finite real tables.

For continuous time, take nested finite partitions containing \(t\) and any prescribed finite collection of readmission thresholds, while isolating \(\infty\), and retain the within-cell order relation.  Apply the finite result and use the quadratic chain theorem to lift each grid coupling to a full law.  The frozen weak-compactness lemma gives a weakly convergent subsequence.  Its limit has the original within-arm margins and is supported on the closed relation \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  The density envelope gives, for finite \(u<v\),
\[
|s_x(u)-s_x(v)|\leq M|u-v|,
\qquad
|K_x(u,B)-K_x(v,B)|
\leq\Pr\{u<D(1)\leq v\mid X=x\}
\leq M|u-v|.                                                         \tag{16}
\]
Thus the discrete suffix minima converge to the continuum infimum, and the limiting coupling attains the requested extrema at the prescribed finite thresholds.

Inside the compact fixed-margin full-law fiber, the set of couplings attaining the upper value at a fixed finite \(r\) is closed.  Indeed, the boundary of the objective event is contained in \(\{D(0)=t\}\cup\{R(1)=r\}\), which has zero probability under the fixed finite-part marginal densities.  The preceding construction gives these closed optimizing sets the finite-intersection property.  Compactness therefore supplies one coupling attaining the upper value for every \(r\leq t\).  Reversing the readmission order supplies one lower coupling for all such \(r\).

Taking \(B=[0,r]\) identifies the upper endpoint as \(A_x^U(r,t)\).  Applying the upper formula to \(B=(r,\infty]\) and subtracting from the selected mass gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_\nu\nu_x(D(0)>t,R(1)\leq r)
&=s-\inf_u\{s-s_x(u)+K_x(u,(r,\infty])\}\\
&=\sup_u\{s_x(u)-K_x(u,(r,\infty])\}
=A_x^L(r,t).                                                         \tag{17}
\end{aligned}
\]

The preceding claims were unstandardized and required no division by \(S(t)\).  Now fix a cohort with \(S(t)\geq\eta\).  By the target-domain definition, \(S(t)>0\), and the finite covariate support permits choosing the common upper, or common lower, extremizer separately in every cell.  Since \(p_x/S(t)\geq0\), summing the cell endpoints and subtracting the fixed \(b_x(r,t)\) gives sharp standardized envelopes \(\theta^L(r,t)\leq\theta_\nu(r,t)\leq\theta^U(r,t)\) for \((r,t)\in\mathcal H_\eta\).

Finally, for \(0\leq a\leq t\), the RM-surface definition gives
\[
-\int_0^a\theta^U(r,t)\,dr
\leq\rho_\nu(a,t)\leq
-\int_0^a\theta^L(r,t)\,dr.                                        \tag{18}
\]
The common upper coupling attains the left endpoint simultaneously along the integral, and the common lower coupling attains the right endpoint.  Thus fixed-cohort RM integration is sharp on \(S(t)\geq\eta\).  If \(S(t)=0\), neither the standardized conditional target nor division by \(S(t)\) is invoked.

The proof is an exact finite-table certificate followed by a quantitatively delimited smoothing construction.  All probabilities are conditional on the sole value of \(X\).  Since \(R(0)=\infty\), the control numerator is zero at every finite readmission threshold.  The four control death rows each have mass \(1/4\), so
\[
S(1)=\frac34,\qquad S(2)=\frac12,\qquad S(3)=\frac14.                \tag{19}
\]
Thus \(0<\eta\leq1/4\) puts \((1,1),(2,2),(3,3)\) in \(\mathcal H_\eta\).

For a feasible projected table \(f=(f_{ij})\), define
\[
A_1=\sum_{i>0}f_{i0},\qquad
A_2=\sum_{\substack{i>1\\j\leq1}}f_{ij},\qquad
A_3=\sum_{j\leq2}f_{3j}.
\]
The singleton capacities from the quadratic chain theorem and the fixed row demands imply
\[
\frac1{20}\leq A_1\leq\kappa^\star_{00}=\frac15,                    \tag{20}
\]
because the other three first-cut columns have total capacity \(7/10\), whereas the demand beyond that cut is \(3/4\).  Likewise,
\[
\frac1{20}\leq A_2\leq\kappa^\star_{10}+\kappa^\star_{11}=\frac14,  \tag{21}
\]
because the second-cut demand is \(1/2\) and columns \(2,3\) have total capacity \(9/20\).  Finally,
\[
\frac1{20}\leq A_3\leq
\kappa^\star_{20}+\kappa^\star_{21}+\kappa^\star_{22}=\frac15,      \tag{22}
\]
where the lower bound follows from \(A_3=1/4-f_{33}\) and \(f_{33}\leq\kappa^\star_{23}=1/5\).

The displayed flows \(f^+\), \(f^-\), and \(f^+\) attain the three upper endpoints, and \(f^-\) attains the lower endpoint in (22).  For the remaining lower endpoints, define
\[
100g^{(1)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
20&0&0&5\\0&15&5&5\\0&0&5&20\\5&5&5&10
\end{pmatrix},\qquad
100g^{(2)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
20&0&0&5\\0&20&0&5\\0&0&10&15\\5&0&5&15
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both have the required row and column margins.  Their complete singleton chain loads, multiplied by \(100\), are
\[
\begin{pmatrix}5&20&15&35\\5&5&10&30\\5&5&5&10\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\begin{pmatrix}5&20&15&35\\5&0&15&30\\5&0&5&15\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Each matrix is entrywise bounded by \(100\kappa^\star\).  The quadratic chain theorem therefore makes both tables feasible, with \(A_1(g^{(1)})=1/20\) and \(A_2(g^{(2)})=1/20\).  The image of the convex flow polytope under each linear coordinate is an interval, so (20)--(22) are the exact intervals.  Dividing by (19), whose denominators are positive, gives
\[
\theta_\nu(1,1)\in\left[\frac1{15},\frac4{15}\right],\quad
\theta_\nu(2,2)\in\left[\frac1{10},\frac12\right],\quad
\theta_\nu(3,3)\in\left[\frac15,\frac45\right].                   \tag{23}
\]

Direct summation of the listed nonzero lift entries gives
\[
100\left(\sum_hq^-_{ihj}\right)_{ij}
=\begin{pmatrix}10&0&10&5\\0&10&5&10\\15&5&0&5\\0&5&0&20\end{pmatrix}
=100f^-,
\]
\[
100\left(\sum_hq^+_{ihj}\right)_{ij}
=\begin{pmatrix}5&0&10&10\\10&15&0&0\\0&0&0&25\\10&5&5&5\end{pmatrix}
=100f^+,
\]
and, for both signs,
\[
100\left(\sum_iq^\pm_{ihj}\right)_{hj}
=\begin{pmatrix}5&0&0&5\\5&10&0&5\\5&5&10&10\\10&5&5&20\end{pmatrix}
=100\mu_1^\star.                                                     \tag{24}
\]
Every listed entry is nonnegative.  Both projected tables have row sums \((25,25,25,25)/100\) and column sums \((25,20,15,40)/100\); attaching \(R(0)=\infty\) therefore gives \(\mu_0^\star\).  Every positive triple has \(i\leq h\), proving \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  Every finite treated readmission category in a positive cell has \(r_j^\star<d_h^\star\), and the control event-order restriction is vacuous.  The complete singleton chain loads are
\[
100\left(\sum_{i>k}f^-_{ij}\right)_{kj}
=\begin{pmatrix}15&20&5&35\\15&10&0&25\\0&5&0&20\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
100\left(\sum_{i>k}f^+_{ij}\right)_{kj}
=\begin{pmatrix}20&20&5&30\\10&5&5&30\\10&5&5&5\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both are entrywise bounded by \(100\kappa^\star\).  Every mark set on the finite carrier is a union of singleton columns, so summing these inequalities certifies all event-set capacities.

Using (19) in the signed direction gives
\[
\ell_\star(\nu)=A_1-A_2+A_3=f_{10}-f_{21}+f_{30}+f_{32}.             \tag{25}
\]
Nonnegativity and the first-cut column-zero and third-cut column-two capacities yield
\[
\ell_\star(\nu)
\leq f_{10}+f_{30}+f_{32}
\leq\kappa^\star_{00}+\kappa^\star_{22}=\frac14.                    \tag{26}
\]
The second-cut column-one capacity and the last-row margin give
\[
f_{21}+f_{31}\leq\frac1{10},
\qquad
f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32}=\frac14-f_{33}\geq\frac1{20}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\ell_\star(\nu)
=f_{10}-(f_{21}+f_{31})+(f_{30}+f_{31}+f_{32})
\geq-\frac1{20}.                                                      \tag{27}
\]
Direct substitution gives \(\ell_\star(f^-)=-1/20\) and \(\ell_\star(f^+)=1/4\).  The full lifts in (24) attain the endpoints, and their mixtures preserve both margins and all support restrictions.  Hence the sharp signed interval is \([-1/20,1/4]\).

The coordinate rectangle generated by (23) has support endpoints
\[
\frac34\frac1{15}-\frac12\frac12+\frac14\frac15=-\frac3{20},
\qquad
\frac34\frac4{15}-\frac12\frac1{10}+\frac14\frac45=\frac7{20}.
\]
Thus its interval \([-3/20,7/20]\) is strictly larger by \(1/10\) at each endpoint.

It remains to delimit the smooth regime.  Fix a nonnegative symmetric \(C^1\) density \(\varphi\) supported on \((-1,1)\), let \(0<\delta<1/8\), and define
\[
\varphi_\delta(u)=\delta^{-1}\varphi(u/\delta),\quad
b_\delta=\|\varphi_\delta\|_\infty,
\quad l_\delta=\|\varphi_\delta'\|_\infty,
\]
\[
M_\delta=\max\{b_\delta,b_\delta^2\},
\qquad
L_\delta=\max\{l_\delta,2b_\delta l_\delta\}.                     \tag{28}
\]
These constants are finite.  Replace each finite category by the corresponding translated bump and retain every \(\infty\) atom.  In a positive lift cell \((i,h,j)\), use independent death draws when \(i<h\), the same death draw when \(i=h\), and an independent readmission draw.  Distinct death centers are at least one unit apart, so \(2\delta<1\) preserves \(D(0)\leq D(1)\); the smallest compatible finite readmission--death gap is \(1/4\), so \(2\delta<1/4\) preserves \(R(1)<D(1)\).  The control readmission remains \(\infty\).

Every finite-part within-arm density is a convex mixture of translates of either \(\varphi_\delta\) or \(\varphi_\delta\otimes\varphi_\delta\).  The former has sup-norm at most \(b_\delta\) and Lipschitz constant at most \(l_\delta\).  For the latter, the product rule and the mean-value inequality give sup-norm at most \(b_\delta^2\) and Lipschitz constant at most \(2b_\delta l_\delta\).  Convex mixtures do not enlarge these bounds.  Equation (28) therefore proves membership in every declared envelope class with
\[
M\geq M_\delta,
\qquad L_{\mathrm{Lip}}\geq L_\delta.                                \tag{29}
\]
This is a nonempty envelope regime; nothing in the construction proves membership when either inequality in (29) fails.

No bump support crosses any threshold \(1,2,3\).  Every numerator, denominator, and cut used in (20)--(27) therefore has its categorical value.  The categorical inequalities remain upper and lower bounds for every smoothed coupling, while the two smoothed full lifts attain the two signed endpoints.  Hence the exact strict support calculation survives smoothing throughout (29).

Finally fix \(\varphi\), \(\delta\), and the incidence pattern, and vary the finitely many mixture weights within the feasible cone.  The relevant threshold support programs have a fixed finite constraint matrix.  Their values are maxima and minima of finitely many affine basic values, hence are continuous and piecewise affine on the feasible weight polytope.  Since each strict gap equals \(1/10\) at the displayed law, both remain positive on a sufficiently small relatively open neighborhood.  The density bounds (29) remain valid because the kernels are fixed and the mixture weights sum to one.  Randomized treatment with probability \(1/2\), degenerate positive \(X\), consistency, and \(C=\tau=3\) give exchangeability, overlap, independent censoring, and \(G_{zx}(u)=1\geq\gamma\) through the full horizon.

The proof uses a closed-relation coupling and coordinate gluing.  Define the latent compatibility class before invoking the observed-law image.  For each \(x\in\mathcal X\), let \(\mathcal Q_x\) be the set of laws on \(\mathcal E^4\) whose \((D(0),R(0))\)-margin is \(\mu_{0x}\), whose \((D(1),R(1))\)-margin is \(\mu_{1x}\), and which assign probability one to \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  The fixed within-arm margins obey the semicompeting-risk order by assumption.  The causal identified set is the set of target surfaces induced by measurable families \((Q_x:x\in\mathcal X)\) with \(Q_x\in\mathcal Q_x\) that reproduce \(P\) under the observed treatment and censoring mechanisms.  This defines the causal target independently of \(\Theta_I(P)\).

Positive covariate-cell support and treatment overlap give \(\Pr_P(Z=z,X=x)>0\).  Full-horizon censoring support gives \(G_{zx}(L)\geq\gamma>0\).  Thus every conditioning operation and inverse weight in the established IPCW-recovery lemma is well defined.  That lemma, using consistency, conditional exchangeability, arm-specific independent censoring, and the support premises, identifies \(\mu_{zx}\), including its horizon atom.  Marginalization then identifies \(d_x\), \(\zeta_x\), \(b_x\), \(K_x\), \(s_x\), and \(S\) as functionals of \(P\).

For necessity, fix \(Q_x\in\mathcal Q_x\), and let \(\nu_x\) be its \((D(0),R(1))\)-margin.  Its margins are \(d_x\) and \(\zeta_x\).  For every \(u\in[0,\tau]\) and Borel \(B\subseteq\mathcal E\), terminal monotonicity gives
\[
\{D(0)>u,R(1)\in B\}
\subseteq
\{D(1)>u,R(1)\in B\}.
\]
Taking probabilities yields
\[
\nu_x((u,\infty]\times B)
\leq\mu_{1x}(D(1)>u,R(1)\in B)=K_x(u,B).
\]
Together with the two margins, these inequalities are exactly \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\).

For sufficiency, fix \(x\) and \(\nu_x\in\mathcal N_x\).  Regard \(\alpha=\nu_x\) and \(\beta=\mu_{1x}\) as laws on two copies of \(\mathcal E^2\).  Their mark margins both equal \(\zeta_x\).  Introduce the closed relation
\[
\mathcal R=\{((d_0,v),(d_1,v')):v=v',\ d_0\leq d_1\}.
\]
The diagonal and the order graph are closed on the compact metric carrier, so \(\mathcal R\) is closed.

The capacity inequalities imply
\[
\alpha([u,\infty]\times B)\leq\beta([u,\infty]\times B)
\qquad(u\in\mathcal E,\ B\in\mathscr B(\mathcal E)).                \tag{1}
\]
For \(0<u\leq\tau\), obtain (1) by taking \(u_k\uparrow u\) in the defining strict-tail inequalities and using continuity from above.  At \(u=0\), (1) is equality of the mark margins.  At \(u=\infty\), it is the defining cut \((\tau,\infty]=\{\infty\}\).

Let \(A\subseteq\mathcal E^2\) be compact and put \(U=\mathcal R(A)\).  The compact-product projection theorem makes \(U\) compact.  For each mark \(v\), its nonempty section is a closed upper interval \([h(v),\infty]\).  For finite \(a\),
\[
\{v:h(v)\leq a\}
=\operatorname{proj}_v\!\left(A\cap([0,a]\times\mathcal E)\right),
\]
which is compact; hence \(h\) is Borel measurable on its domain.  Round finite \(h(v)\) downward on nested grids, retaining empty and \(\infty\) sections.  The resulting sets \(U_n\) decrease to \(U\), and each \(U_n\) is a finite disjoint union of \([q,\infty]\times B_{nq}\) with Borel, pairwise disjoint mark sets.  Summing (1) over those pieces and passing to the decreasing limit gives
\[
\alpha(A)\leq\alpha(U)\leq\beta(U)=\beta(\mathcal R(A)).             \tag{2}
\]
The frozen Strassen closed-relation lemma applied to (2) supplies a coupling of \((D(0),R(1))\sim\nu_x\) and \((D(1),R'(1))\sim\mu_{1x}\) supported on \(R(1)=R'(1)\) and \(D(0)\leq D(1)\).  Identifying the equal marks gives a law \(\pi_x\) of \((D(0),D(1),R(1))\).

Reorder \(\mu_{0x}\) as the law of \((R(0),D(0))\).  It and \(\pi_x\) have the same \(D(0)\)-margin \(d_x\).  The established compact-coordinate gluing lemma gives a law \(Q_x\) of \((R(0),D(0),D(1),R(1))\) satisfying
\[
\mathcal L_{Q_x}(D(0),R(0))=\mu_{0x},\qquad
\mathcal L_{Q_x}(D(1),R(1))=\mu_{1x},\qquad
Q_x\{D(0)\leq D(1)\}=1.                                            \tag{3}
\]

prose_updates.tldr: Death truncates readmission, so the two-index TV-SACE and RM-SACE surfaces depend on an unidentified cross-world assignment of treated readmission times to control death times. Under arm-specific independent censoring through the full horizon and the additional maintained order \(D(0)\le D(1)\), the note characterizes the complete sharp monotonicity-restricted surface by a necessary-and-sufficient marked-capacity lift, proves common fixed-cohort extremizers and exact RM integration, and gives a certified three-horizon law whose joint cross-cohort support is strictly narrower than its coordinate rectangle. Quadratic chain flows, qualitative continuous-grid convergence, and deterministic-grid finite-sample outer containment make the population characterization computable. A joint marked-product-limit/IPCW functional limit, root-\(n\) grid-bias control, and simultaneous multiplier bands remain open.
